title: What Lasts Is Not What Can Be Learned

scenes.tts: Do people have windows like a songbird's? And what does an age curve tell us?
scenes.visual: Title card: What Lasts Is Not What Can Be Learned. A child's silhouette beside a sparrow.
scenes.narration: Do people have windows like a songbird's? And what does an age curve tell us?

scenes.tts: In nineteen sixty-seven, Eric Lenneberg proposed a critical period for language, from early childhood to puberty.
scenes.caption: In 1967, Eric Lenneberg proposed a critical period for language, from early childhood to puberty.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Eric Lenneberg, 1967. A timeline from early childhood to puberty, shaded as the proposed window.
scenes.narration: In 1967, Eric Lenneberg proposed a critical period for language, from early childhood to puberty.

scenes.tts: The main natural test is deaf children of hearing parents who first meet a signed language late.
scenes.visual: A child signing with a teacher; a timeline marks late first exposure to sign.
scenes.narration: The main natural test is deaf children of hearing parents who first meet a signed language late.

scenes.tts: Delayed access to sign does affect later proficiency.
scenes.visual: Card: delayed access to sign affects later proficiency. Credit: Newport, 1990.
scenes.narration: Delayed access to sign does affect later proficiency.

scenes.tts: Mayberry compared adults who learned sign at the same age. Some already had English before losing their hearing.
scenes.visual: Two adults with the same age of learning sign. Labels: no accessible language before sign (sign as a first language); English before sign (sign as a second language). Credit: Mayberry, 1993.
scenes.narration: Mayberry compared adults who learned sign at the same age. Some already had English before losing their hearing.

scenes.tts: Those with no accessible language before sign did worse. The groups also differed in when they lost hearing, so it is not a perfect control. But it suggests missing early language, not only age, leaves a lasting mark.
scenes.visual: The first-language bar sits lower than the second-language bar. Card: missing early language, not only age.
scenes.narration: Those with no accessible language before sign did worse. The groups also differed in when they lost hearing, so it is not a perfect control. But it suggests missing early language, not only age, leaves a lasting mark.

scenes.tts: Johnson and Newport tested English grammar in adults who arrived in the United States at ages three to thirty-nine.
scenes.caption: Johnson and Newport tested English grammar in adults who arrived in the United States at ages 3 to 39.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Johnson and Newport, 1989. Empty axes: grammar score against age of arrival, 3 to 39. On screen: 46 adults, first language Korean or Chinese.
scenes.narration: Johnson and Newport tested English grammar in adults who arrived in the United States at ages 3 to 39.

scenes.tts: Predict. Plot adult grammar scores against age of arrival. Do scores hold until puberty, then drop? Or fall earlier?
scenes.visual: Two ghost curves on the axes, labelled possible adult scores (outcome, not learning ability): flat, then dropping at puberty; falling from childhood. Question mark.
scenes.narration: Predict. Plot adult grammar scores against age of arrival. Do scores hold until puberty, then drop? Or fall earlier?

scenes.tts: Early arrivals scored like native speakers. Then scores fell steadily with later arrival, up to about puberty.
scenes.visual: Points build by age of arrival: arrivals at 3 to 7 sit at native level; points then fall steadily toward puberty.
scenes.narration: Early arrivals scored like native speakers. Then scores fell steadily with later arrival, up to about puberty.

scenes.tts: Later arrivals scored lower, and varied widely. The outcome curve was graded, falling from childhood.
scenes.visual: Points after puberty scatter widely at a lower level. The falling-from-childhood outcome curve fits. Label: what lasts, not learning ability.
scenes.narration: Later arrivals scored lower, and varied widely. The outcome curve was graded, falling from childhood.

scenes.tts: But a huge online grammar quiz suggested that grammar-learning ability stays high until about seventeen.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Hartshorne, Tenenbaum and Pinker, 2018. On screen: about 670,000 people. A learning-ability line, flat and high until about 17, then declining.
scenes.narration: But a huge online grammar quiz suggested that grammar-learning ability stays high until about seventeen.

scenes.tts: So how can a twelve-year-old arrive with full learning ability, yet end below native level?
scenes.visual: A 12-year-old arrives on the timeline under the flat, high part of the ability line. Question mark over the final grammar score.
scenes.narration: So how can a twelve-year-old arrive with full learning ability, yet end below native level?

scenes.tts: Grammar takes years to learn. A later starter gets fewer full-speed years before the slowdown.
scenes.visual: Bar timeline for starts at 5, 10, 12, 14 and 25. Full-speed years before 17 shaded: 12, 7, 5, 3 and 0. A dashed line at 7 years marks the toy's assumed need. Note: a toy calculation, not data.
scenes.narration: Grammar takes years to learn. A later starter gets fewer full-speed years before the slowdown.

scenes.tts: Suppose, as a toy, native-like grammar takes seven full-speed years. A twelve-year-old gets only five.
scenes.caption: Suppose, as a toy, native-like grammar takes 7 full-speed years. A 12-year-old gets only 5.
scenes.visual: The 12 bar highlights: 5 shaded years against the dashed line at 7. Label: 2 years short.
scenes.narration: Suppose, as a toy, native-like grammar takes 7 full-speed years. A 12-year-old gets only 5.

scenes.tts: If later learning is slow enough, that shortfall lasts.
scenes.visual: After 17 the 12 bar keeps growing, but slowly, and stays below the dashed line.
scenes.narration: If later learning is slow enough, that shortfall lasts.

scenes.tts: So what lasts can start to fall before the ability to learn does.
scenes.visual: Two curves on one plot: lasting grammar falling from childhood; learning ability flat until about 17.
scenes.narration: So what lasts can start to fall before the ability to learn does.

scenes.tts: A curve of what lasts is not a curve of learning ability. Why learning slows is still debated.
scenes.visual: Card: a curve of what lasts is not a curve of learning ability. Below: candidates, plasticity, an entrenched first language, input.
scenes.narration: A curve of what lasts is not a curve of learning ability. Why learning slows is still debated.

scenes.tts: In sight, infants treated for dense cataracts showed some improvement in acuity after as little as an hour.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Maurer, Lewis, Brent and Levin, 1999. An acuity plot: at treatment, on the newborn line; a small rise after an hour of patterned input.
scenes.narration: In sight, infants treated for dense cataracts showed some improvement in acuity after as little as an hour.

scenes.tts: Yet processing of the spacing between facial features stayed impaired years later. Separate abilities have separate windows.
scenes.visual: A separate panel: two faces differing only in the spacing of their features; a lasting deficit years after early deprivation. Label: separate windows.
scenes.narration: Yet processing of the spacing between facial features stayed impaired years later. Separate abilities have separate windows.

scenes.tts: So ask what input arrives, at what age, and what lasts.
scenes.visual: Closing card: What input arrives? At what age? What lasts?
scenes.narration: So ask what input arrives, at what age, and what lasts.
